title: The quadruped backbone is a double-armed cantilever girder, not an arch

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The quadruped backbone is a double-armed cantilever girder, not an arch

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because the jointed legs cannot resist the horizontal thrust of an arch and there is no tie between its ends, the backbone of a standing quadruped is not an arch, tied arch or bowstring girder but is mechanically comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The structure is not an arch, nor a tied arch, nor a bowstring girder: but it is strictly and beautifully comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVI, “On Form and Mechanical Efficiency”; topic “Quadruped skeleton as a bridge”. Scope: vertebral column and associated ligaments of standing quadrupeds

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch16-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The competing structural analogies can be formalized, although biological joints and active muscles depart from simple bridge models. Public morphology enables restricted modeling, but decisive paired force data are limited.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Build musculoskeletal free-body models of standing quadrupeds and compare force transmission and horizontal thrust under arch, tied-arch and double-cantilever idealizations. The model class that uniquely matches measured reactions and ligament strains provides the test.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Static anatomy alone does not identify structural load paths.

Open ligament-force and ground-reaction data are sparse across species.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Skeletal geometry is openly scanned and horse ground reactions are deposited, so the rival structural models can be compared in a restricted set of quadrupeds. Ligament lines of action and material properties still have to be compiled. The exercise can reject a naive masonry arch for the horse and does not yet decide the analogy across standing quadrupeds.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Build arch, tied-arch and double-cantilever models on the same quadruped skeletal geometry and compare their horizontal thrust and moment diagrams with measured ground reaction forces and with the presence or absence of a ventral tie. The cantilever would be favoured if the limbs do not supply the arch's thrust and the spine's moments match a double-supported beam; a large horizontal thrust carried by the legs would favour the arch.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Muscles and ligaments act as time-varying ties, so a standing elastic analogy misses the dynamic case.

Open force data are concentrated on horses and a few other gait-lab species.
